items.question: "Ancient Andhra was one of the great heartlands of Indian Buddhism." Discuss with reference to the patronage of the Satavahanas and Ikshvakus, the major Buddhist sites of the region, and the contribution of Acharya Nagarjuna.
items.modelAnswer:
From the last centuries BCE to about the 6th century CE, the lower **Krishna–Godavari valley of Andhra** was among the most vibrant Buddhist regions of India, sustained by royal wealth, maritime trade and a remarkable school of art.

**Royal patronage.** Under the **Satavahanas** — the 'Andhras' of the Puranas — the eastern centre at **Dhanyakataka/Dharanikota** near Amaravati became a great religious focus; tradition even holds that the **Buddha expounded the Kalachakra at Dhanyakataka**. Though the Satavahana kings performed Vedic sacrifices, they and their queens freely endowed Buddhist monks with land. The succeeding **Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda)** show the same pattern in sharper form: the **kings remained Brahmanical** (agnihotra, vajapeya, ashvamedha) while the **royal women — notably Chamtisiri —** were lavish Buddhist donors, funding the Mahachaitya and monasteries.

**Sites and art.** Andhra has one of India's **densest clusters of Buddhist remains** — **Amaravati** and **Nagarjunakonda** (Krishna valley), **Bhattiprolu** (whose inscribed relic caskets preserve an early southern Brahmi, the Bhattiprolu script), **Salihundam** on the Vamsadhara in the Kalinga borderland, **Ghantasala**, **Jaggayyapeta**, **Guntupalli**, and the Visakhapatnam hill-monasteries of **Thotlakonda, Bavikonda and Sankaram**. The **Amaravati school of art**, working in white limestone, produced crowded narrative reliefs that rank with Gandhara and Mathura and **influenced Sri Lanka and South-East Asia** — a link confirmed by the excavated **monastery for Sri Lankan monks** at Nagarjunakonda.

**Acharya Nagarjuna.** The region's greatest intellectual contribution was **Acharya Nagarjuna**, founder of the **Madhyamika** school and its doctrine of **Sunyavada** (emptiness), author of the *Mula-madhyamaka-karika*, and traditionally associated with **Sriparvata**. His dialectic shaped later Indian philosophy, including Sankara's Advaita.

**Conclusion.** Sustained by Satavahana and Ikshvaku patronage, enriched by a world-class art school, and crowned by Nagarjuna's philosophy, ancient Andhra was both a Buddhist power-house and a bridge that carried the faith across the seas — a heritage still visible in its stupas and museums today.
keyPoints: Krishna-Godavari valley = a major Buddhist heartland, c.2nd c BCE-6th c CE.
Satavahana centre Dhanyakataka; tradition of the Buddha's Kalachakra teaching there.
Ikshvaku kings Vedic (ashvamedha) but royal women (Chamtisiri) major Buddhist patrons.
Site cluster: Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Salihundam, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Guntupalli, Thotlakonda/Bavikonda/Sankaram.
Amaravati art school (white limestone) influenced Sri Lanka & SE Asia; Sri Lankan monks' vihara at Nagarjunakonda.

items.question: Trace the political succession in coastal Andhra from the decline of the Satavahanas to the rise of the Eastern Chalukyas, highlighting the roles of the Ikshvakus, Salankayanas and Vishnukundins.
items.modelAnswer:
The break-up of the **Satavahana empire** in the 3rd century CE opened a long phase in which a series of regional dynasties held the fertile **Krishna–Godavari region**, steadily shifting the political nucleus of coastal Andhra towards **Vengi**.

**Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri (3rd–4th c CE).** The earliest successors in the eastern Krishna valley were the **Andhra Ikshvakus**, ruling from **Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda)**. Their line ran **Vasishthiputra Chamtamula → Virapurushadatta → Ehuvala Chamtamula → Rudrapurushadatta**. They combined **Vedic kingship** with famous **Buddhist patronage by their women**, and left one of India's richest Buddhist campuses before fading in the 4th century.

**Salankayanas of Vengi (c.300–440 CE).** Power then passed to the **Salankayanas**, who ruled the **Godavari–Krishna doab** from **Vengi (Pedavegi, near Eluru)** under the **bull (Nandi) emblem**, at first as Pallava feudatories and later independently.

**Vishnukundins (5th–7th c CE).** The **Vishnukundins** **wrested coastal Andhra from the Salankayanas**; their greatest ruler **Madhava Varma** performed **Vedic sacrifices including the ashvamedha**, and the dynasty is associated with capitals such as **Denduluru**. To this period belong the early rock-cut cave temples of **Undavalli, Mogalrajapuram and Bhairavakonda**, marking the growth of Brahmanical architecture beside the older Buddhist tradition.

**Transition to the Eastern Chalukyas.** Vishnukundin rule ended when the Badami Chalukya **Pulakeshin II** conquered the eastern Deccan and installed his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana**, who founded the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (from 624 CE)** — a dynasty that would dominate Andhra for centuries and nurture the birth of Telugu literature.

**Conclusion.** The sequence **Dhanyakataka (Satavahanas) → Vijayapuri (Ikshvakus) → Vengi (Salankayanas → Vishnukundins) → Eastern Chalukyas** shows both the political fragmentation after the Satavahanas and the enduring pull of Vengi as the heart of coastal Andhra.
keyPoints: Satavahana decline (3rd c CE) opened a phase of regional Andhra dynasties.
Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda): Chamtamula -> Virapurushadatta -> Ehuvala -> Rudrapurushadatta.
Salankayanas (c.300-440 CE) ruled Godavari-Krishna doab from Vengi/Pedavegi; bull emblem.
Vishnukundins (5th-7th c CE): Madhava Varma (ashvamedha); Undavalli/Mogalrajapuram/Bhairavakonda caves.
Pulakeshin II ended them; Kubja Vishnuvardhana founded the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (624 CE).
Overall shift of the political centre towards Vengi.
